document.title: The Pentagon Disinformation That Fueled America's UFO Mythology (The Wall Street Journal, 2025)
document.author: Joel Schectman and Aruna Viswanatha

passages.text: At times, as with the deception around Area 51, military officers spread false documents to create a smokescreen for real secret-weapons programs. In other cases, officials allowed UFO myths to take root in the interest of national security—for instance, to prevent the Soviet Union from detecting vulnerabilities in the systems protecting nuclear installations. Stories tended to take on a life of their own, such as the three-decade journey of a purported piece of space metal that turned out to be nothing of the sort. And one long-running practice was more like a fraternity hazing ritual that spun wildly out of control.

This account is based on interviews with two dozen current and former U.S. officials, scientists and military contractors involved in the inquiry, as well as thousands of pages of documents, recordings, emails and text messages.

It turned out the witnesses had been victims of a bizarre hazing ritual.For decades, certain new commanders of the Air Force’s most classified programs, as part of their induction briefings, would be handed a piece of paper with a photo of what looked like a flying saucer. The craft was described as an antigravity maneuvering vehicle.The officers were told that the program they were joining, dubbed Yankee Blue, was part of an effort to reverse-engineer the technology on the craft. They were told never to mention it again. Many never learned it was fake.

Could this be the basis for the persistent belief that the U.S. has an alien program that we’ve concealed from the American people? Haines wanted to know, according to people familiar with the matter. How extensive was it? she asked.

In a statement, a Defense Department spokeswoman acknowledged that AARO had uncovered evidence of fake classified program materials relating to extraterrestrials, and had briefed lawmakers and intelligence officials. The spokeswoman, Sue Gough, said the department didn’t include that information in its report last year because the investigation wasn’t completed, but expects to provide it in another report scheduled for later this year.
In 1967, Robert Salas, now 84, was an Air Force captain sitting in a walk-in closet-sized bunker, manning the controls of 10 nuclear missiles in Montana.

Kirkpatrick’s team dug into the story and discovered a terrestrial explanation. The barriers of concrete and steel surrounding America’s nuclear missiles were thick enough to give them a chance if hit first by a Soviet strike. But scientists at the time feared the intense storm of electromagnetic waves generated by a nuclear detonation might render the hardware needed to launch a counterstrike unusable.To test this vulnerability, the Air Force developed an exotic electromagnetic generator that simulated this pulse of disruptive energy without the need to detonate a nuclear weapon.When activated, this device, placed on a portable platform 60 feet above the facility, would gather power until it glowed, sometimes with a blinding orange light. It would then fire a burst of energy that could resemble lightning.The electromagnetic pulses snaked down cables connected to the bunker where launch commanders like Salas sat, disrupting the guidance systems, disabling the weapons and haunting the men to this day.But any public leak of the tests at the time would have allowed Russia to know that America’s nuclear arsenal could be disabled in a first strike. The witnesses were kept in the dark.To this day Salas believes he was party to an intergalactic intervention to stop nuclear war which the government has tried to hide. He is half right.

quotes.quote: In 1967, Robert Salas, now 84, was an Air Force captain sitting in a walk-in closet-sized bunker, manning the controls of 10 nuclear missiles in Montana.
Kirkpatrick’s team dug into the story and discovered a terrestrial explanation.
To test this vulnerability, the Air Force developed an exotic electromagnetic generator that simulated this pulse of disruptive energy without the need to detonate a nuclear weapon.
When activated, this device, placed on a portable platform 60 feet above the facility, would gather power until it glowed, sometimes with a blinding orange light.
The electromagnetic pulses snaked down cables connected to the bunker where launch commanders like Salas sat, disrupting the guidance systems, disabling the weapons and haunting the men to this day.
The witnesses were kept in the dark.

differs: The article gives the EMP explanation as the finding of Sean Kirkpatrick's AARO team: "Kirkpatrick’s team dug into the story and discovered a terrestrial explanation", an Air Force "exotic electromagnetic generator" that "simulated this pulse of disruptive energy without the need to detonate a nuclear weapon", set "on a portable platform 60 feet above the facility", whose pulses "snaked down cables connected to the bunker where launch commanders like Salas sat". The tellers read this as the reporters' own explanation; in the text it is the reporters' account of what the investigators found, resting, by the article's own statement, on "interviews with two dozen current and former U.S. officials, scientists and military contractors involved in the inquiry" and documents it does not name.

document.title: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2025 (SA 3111 to S. 2296)

passages.text: SA 3111. Mr. SCHUMER (for himself, Mr. Rounds, and Mrs. Gillibrand) submitted an amendment intended to be proposed by him to the bill S. 2296, to authorize appropriations for fiscal year 2026 for military activities of the Department of Defense, for military construction, and for defense activities of the Department of Energy, to prescribe military personnel strengths for such fiscal year, and for other purposes; which was ordered to lie on the table; as follows:
This division may be cited as the ``Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2025'' or the ``UAP Disclosure Act of 2025''.

quotes.quote: SA 3111. Mr. SCHUMER (for himself, Mr. Rounds, and Mrs. Gillibrand) submitted an amendment intended to be proposed by him to the bill S. 2296, to authorize appropriations for fiscal year 2026 for military activities of the Department of Defense, for military construction, and for defense activities of the Department of Energy, to prescribe military personnel strengths for such fiscal year, and for other purposes; which was ordered to lie on the table; as follows:
This division may be cited as the ``Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2025'' or the ``UAP Disclosure Act of 2025''.

differs: In the Congressional Record of 29 July 2025 the UAP Disclosure Act of 2025 is printed as an amendment (SA 3111) that Schumer "submitted" for himself, Rounds and Gillibrand to S. 2296, the Senate's defence authorization bill for fiscal year 2026, "which was ordered to lie on the table". The Record of that day shows the bill brought back to the Senate as a submitted amendment; the teller's forecast that the Senate would pass it goes a step beyond what this page records.

differs: The UAP sections of the law enacted on 22 December 2023 have the Archivist set up "a collection of unidentified anomalous phenomena ... records in the National Archives", have "each head of a Government office" identify and prepare such records for it, and let disclosure be postponed on the original classification authority's finding of "clear and convincing evidence" of harm. The Senate's UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (SA 797) had given "Witnesses, close observers, and whistleblowers providing information directly to the Review Board" the protections of 50 U.S.C. 3373b(b) through an independent Review Board, and the enacted sections set up no such board; the teller does not say which protections he means, and if they are these, the law shows the end state of the conference he calls a reconciliation, not the bargaining that led to it.

document.title: Analysis of Reports of Unidentified Aerial Objects (Project Blue Book Special Report No. 14)
document.issuer: Air Technical Intelligence Center, United States Air Force

passages.text: Object sightings All sightings Unit sightings 2199 =100% 3201 = 100% 2554 =100%
Unknown 434=19.7%

Thus, the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS considered in this study are "flying saucers'' is concluded to be extremely small, since the most complete and reliable reports from the present data, when isolated and studied, conclusively failed to reveal even a rough model, and since the data as a whole failed to reveal any marked patterns or trends. Therefore, on the basis of this evaluation of the information, it is considered to be highly improbable that any of the reports of unidentified aerial objects examined in this study represent observations of technological developments outside the range of present-day scientific knowledge.

quotes.quote: Unknown 434=19.7%

Thus, the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS considered in this study are "flying saucers'' is concluded to be extremely small, since the most complete and reliable reports from the present data, when isolated and studied, conclusively failed to reveal even a rough model, and since the data as a whole failed to reveal any marked patterns or trends.

Therefore, on the basis of this evaluation of the information, it is considered to be highly improbable that any of the reports of unidentified aerial objects examined in this study represent observations of technological developments outside the range of present-day scientific knowledge.

differs: In the report's own figure of evaluations the unknowns are "Unknown 434=19.7%" of 2,199 object sightings, within 3,201 sighting reports in all; the teller's "21%" is near that share, while his count of "almost a thousand" cases is none of the report's bases. The report itself concludes that "the probability that any of the UNKNOWNS considered in this study are "flying saucers'' is concluded to be extremely small" and that it is "highly improbable" that any report shows "technological developments outside the range of present-day scientific knowledge": the step from its data table to a finding the press release hid is the teller's reading, set against the report's own conclusion.

document.title: The Epic of Gilgamish, Tablet XI (translated by E. A. Wallis Budge in The Babylonian Story of the Deluge)

quotes.quote: The mass of tablets which had been discovered by Layard and Rassam at Nineveh came to the British Museum in 1854-5, and their examination by Rawlinson and Norris began very soon after.
quotes.locator: Introduction, George Smith's Discovery of the Epic of Gilgamish and the Story of the Deluge

quotes.quote: In that year the Trustees of the British Museum employed George Smith to assist Rawlinson in sorting, classifying and rejoining fragments, and a comprehensive examination of the collection by him began.
quotes.locator: Introduction, George Smith's Discovery of the Epic of Gilgamish and the Story of the Deluge

quotes.quote: he discovered among other important documents (1) a series of portions of tablets which give the adventures of Gilgamish, an ancient king of Erech; (2) An account of the Deluge, which is supplied by the Eleventh Tablet of the Legend of Gilgamish (in more than one version);
quotes.locator: Introduction, George Smith's Discovery of the Epic of Gilgamish and the Story of the Deluge

quotes.quote: it was not until December, 1872, that George Smith published his description of the Legend of Gilgamish, and a translation of the "Chaldean Account of the Deluge."
quotes.locator: Introduction, George Smith's Discovery of the Epic of Gilgamish and the Story of the Deluge

quotes.quote: During the excavations which Smith carried out at Kuyûnjik in 1873 and 1874 he recovered many fragments of tablets, the texts of which enabled him to complete his description of the contents of the Twelve Tablets of the Legend of Gilgamish which included his translation of the story of the Deluge.
quotes.locator: Introduction, George Smith's Discovery of the Epic of Gilgamish and the Story of the Deluge

quotes.quote: Unfortunately Smith died of hunger and sickness near Aleppo in 1876
quotes.locator: Introduction, George Smith's Discovery of the Epic of Gilgamish and the Story of the Deluge

differs: In the introduction to The Babylonian Story of the Deluge, Budge writes that the tablets "discovered by Layard and Rassam at Nineveh came to the British Museum in 1854-5", that the Trustees "employed George Smith" in 1866 to sort and rejoin them, that he found among them the Gilgamish tablets and the Deluge account, published in December 1872, and that "During the excavations which Smith carried out at Kuyûnjik in 1873 and 1874 he recovered many fragments" before he died in 1876. In this account the first tablets reached the museum through Layard and Rassam, and Smith's own finds at Nineveh are the further fragments of 1873 and 1874; the teller's picture of Smith bringing the tablets to the museum fits those later fragments, not the collection he first read. His years on the tablets run from 1866 to 1876, close to the teller's ten.
